accounting.accounting_cycle.recap:
The accounting cycle is the fixed route every transaction travels: source documents, journals, posting to the ledger, trial balance, final accounts, financial statements. The order is not decoration - each stage runs on the output of the one before it, which is why no stage can be skipped or swapped.

Source documents come first because accounting records nothing without evidence: a till slip, an invoice, a bank statement proves the date, amount and parties. The journals - books of first entry - then sort transactions into daily lists by type: cash in through the Cash Receipts Journal, cash out through the Cash Payments Journal, credit sales and purchases through their own journals. Sorting first means only column totals move on, not hundreds of individual entries.

Posting transfers those journal totals into the general ledger, where information is reorganised by account instead of by date. Every posting follows double entry - each amount debits one account and credits another - and each account is then balanced, giving one clean figure per item: total sales, cash on hand, amounts owed.

The trial balance lists every ledger balance in a debit or credit column. Because double entry forces every debit to have an equal credit, the two columns must agree. If they do not, an error exists in the recording or posting. Note the limit: a balancing trial balance proves arithmetic equality only - an amount posted to the wrong account on the correct side still balances.

At year end, the final accounts calculate profit inside the ledger: Sales and Cost of Sales close off to the Trading account, which produces gross profit; gross profit and all other incomes and expenses close off to the Profit and Loss account, which produces net profit; net profit transfers to Capital, because profit belongs to the owner. Finally, the financial statements report the results: the Statement of Comprehensive Income shows incomes, expenses and profit for the period; the Statement of Financial Position shows assets, equity and liabilities on the closing date.

The stages run on different clocks: documents and journals daily, posting and the trial balance monthly, final accounts and statements yearly - then the whole route repeats for the next period, which is why it is called a cycle. Quick self-test: for any stage, name what it receives from the previous stage and what it hands to the next. If you can do that for all six, you own the cycle.

The total of the Cash Receipts Journal

accounting.control_accounts.recap:
A control account is a one-account summary of a whole group of people the business deals with. The Debtors Control account in the general ledger carries the totals for all debtors as a group, while each debtor's personal detail lives in a separate book, the Debtors Ledger. The rule that runs everything: whatever is posted to the personal accounts in detail must be posted to the control account in total - journal totals only, never individual invoices.

Debtors are an asset, so the account grows on the debit side and shrinks on the credit side. For every entry, ask one question: did this event make debtors owe us more, or less? Credit sales (the Debtors Journal total) make debtors owe more - debit the control account. Everything that reduces the debt goes on the credit side: payments received from debtors (the debtors column of the Cash Receipts Journal), goods returned or allowances granted (the Debtors Allowances Journal), and bad debts written off. A bad debt is credited even though no money arrives - the business stops counting an amount it will never collect, and the contra account is Bad Debts, an expense.

Balance the account like any ledger account: total both sides, insert the balancing figure as "Balance c/d", and bring it down. A debit balance states what all debtors together still owe.

The pay-off is the built-in check. At month end, list every individual debtor's balance from the Debtors Ledger and add the list. That total must equal the control account balance - two independent routes built from the same transactions. If they differ, an error exists somewhere: an invoice missed in a journal total, a receipt posted twice, a casting error. The disagreement does not name the error; it proves one exists and tells you to hunt.

The Creditors Control account is the mirror image. Creditors are a liability, so the balance sits on the credit side: credit purchases make the business owe more (credit the account); payments to creditors and returns to suppliers make it owe less (debit the account). Its balance must agree with the list of creditors' balances from the Creditors Ledger. Master the debtors version, flip every side, and creditors comes free.

accounting.double_entry.recap:
Everything a business owns was funded by somebody: either the owner or an outsider. What it owns are assets (A); the owner's funding is owner's equity (O); outsiders' funding is liabilities (L). That fact is the accounting equation, A = O + L, and it must hold after every single transaction. If it stops balancing, an error was made.

The equation connects to the ledger through the sides: assets increase on the debit side; owner's equity and liabilities increase on the credit side; decreases go on the opposite side in each case. The double-entry principle then says every transaction affects at least two accounts, with total debits equal to total credits - which is exactly what keeps the equation in balance.

Analyse any transaction in five steps. One: name the two accounts affected. Two: classify each as asset, owner's equity or liability. Three: decide whether each increases or decreases. Four: apply the sides - asset up means debit; O or L up means credit; decreases reverse. Five: confirm the equation still balances.

Run the classic set. Owner deposits R100 000 capital: Bank (asset) up - debit; Capital (equity) up - credit; both sides of the equation rise R100 000. Buy equipment for R30 000 cash: Equipment up - debit; Bank down - credit; an asset swap, net effect on A is zero, but both entries are still recorded. Buy stock on credit for R12 000: Trading Stock up - debit; Creditors Control (liability) up - credit; A and L rise together. Pay a creditor R5 000: Creditors Control down - debit; Bank down - credit; A and L fall together. Every case: one debit, one credit, equation intact.

Incomes and expenses are not a fourth element - they are movements inside owner's equity. Income increases O, so it is recorded on the credit side; expenses decrease O, so they are debited. Paid wages R2 000: debit Wages (O down via an expense), credit Bank (asset down).

Final habit: debit does not mean good or bad - debit and credit are just the left and right sides, and the business's point of view is the only one recorded. Analyse with the five steps every time and no transaction can surprise you.

accounting.gaap_principles.recap:
GAAP - Generally Accepted Accounting Practice - is the shared rulebook that makes financial statements trustworthy and comparable. Grade 10 needs six principles, and exams almost never ask for definitions: they give a scenario and ask which principle is applied. So learn each rule with its tell-tale sign.

Historical cost: assets are recorded at their original, verifiable purchase price, not today's estimated value. The purchase price is a fact backed by a source document; market value is a shifting opinion. Sign: an asset "now worth more" but "still shown at" what it cost.

Prudence: never overstate good news, never understate bad news - anticipate possible losses, never record profits before they are certain. Writing off doubtful debts and valuing damaged stock at the lower figure are prudence at work. Sign: a cautious choice made under uncertainty. Do not confuse it with historical cost: historical cost sticks to an original price; prudence picks the careful estimate when the outcome is uncertain.

Materiality: information is material if leaving it out or misstating it would change a reader's decision. A R45 stapler that lasts years is simply expensed - too small to matter - while a delivery vehicle is a fixed asset tracked separately. Sign: a decision turning on whether an amount is big enough to matter.

Business entity rule: the business and its owner are separate in the books. The owner's personal spending from business funds is Drawings, never a business expense; the owner's private car and house never appear among business assets. Sign: any brush between the owner's personal affairs and the business records - "the owner took", "for personal use".

Going concern: the books assume the business will keep operating into the foreseeable future - which justifies recording assets at cost for continued use and spreading costs over future years. Sign: statements prepared "assuming the business will continue".

Matching: incomes and expenses belong to the period in which they occur, so a period's expenses are matched against that period's income for a fair profit. Insurance paid in advance is split between years; wages owed at year end are accrued into the year they were worked. Sign: amounts shifted between periods - prepaid, accrued, "belongs to this year".

Exam method: underline the action taken, then ask what the accountant is refusing to do or insisting on doing. The refusal points straight at the principle.

options: An injection - foreign money flows into South African firms
A leakage - the wine leaves the country

economics.circular_flow_basics.recap:
The circular flow maps how money and resources move between an economy's participants. Households own the factors of production - natural resources, labour, capital, entrepreneurship - and supply them to firms through the factor market. Firms pay factor incomes in return: rent, wages, interest and profit. Households then spend that income buying goods and services from firms through the goods market, and the circle turns. Every real flow (factors, goods) has a money flow (income, spending) travelling in the opposite direction.

Money escapes the spending stream through leakages and returns through injections, and each pair travels through the same door. Door one, the financial sector: households save part of their income - a leakage - but banks lend those savings to firms, which buy machinery and buildings - investment, an injection. Door two, the government: taxes drain spending power from households and firms - a leakage - while government spending on salaries, grants, roads and services pumps it back - an injection. Door three, the foreign sector: paying for imports sends money out of the country - a leakage - while export earnings bring foreign money in - an injection. Adding the foreign sector is what turns a closed economy into an open one, which is what South Africa is.

The three leakages are savings, taxes and imports; the three injections are investment, government spending and exports. Classify any transaction by following the money's direction, not the goods: money leaving the domestic spending stream is a leakage; money entering it is an injection. Buying an imported television is a leakage even though the television arrives, because the payment leaves.

The comparison between totals decides the economy's direction. If leakages exceed injections, less money returns to firms each round: production, income and employment shrink. If injections exceed leakages, the flow expands. When they are equal, the economy is in equilibrium. And resist the trap of calling leakages "bad" - savings finance tomorrow's investment; leakage and injection describe direction of flow, not virtue.

diagnostic.prompt: Total cost is R60 at 3 units and R76 at 4 units. The marginal cost of the fourth unit is:
A price-taking firm sells at R30. The next unit has marginal cost R38. The firm should:
options: Refuse the unit - it would reduce profit by R8
Produce it only if average cost is below R30

economics.cost_and_revenue_analysis.recap:
Cost and revenue analysis turns a plain output-and-total-cost table into a production decision. Start with the cost side. Total cost at zero output is the fixed cost - rent and insurance are owed even when nothing is produced - and it hides inside every later total; the growing remainder is variable cost.

Two derived measures, two different verbs. Average cost = total cost DIVIDED by output: the cost per unit so far. It falls at first as the fixed cost spreads over more units, bottoms out, then rises as capacity strains - the U-shape. Marginal cost = the SUBTRACTION of neighbouring totals: what the last unit alone added. Marginal cost typically dips and then climbs steeply. Divide for average, subtract for marginal - mixing the verbs is the classic error.

The revenue side is simple for a price taker. At a market price of R30: total revenue climbs by R30 per unit; average revenue equals the price (revenue per unit sold can only be the selling price); and marginal revenue - the extra revenue from one more unit - is also R30 every time, because selling more does not move the market price. Graphed, that flat line at the price is the firm's demand line, the signature of perfect competition.

The decision rule: profit is maximised at the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost - produce every unit whose MR is at least its MC, and refuse the first unit whose MC overtakes MR. Reason unit by unit: a unit bringing R30 at a marginal cost of R26 adds R4 of profit - produce it; a unit costing R38 against R30 destroys R8 - refuse it, even if the firm remains profitable overall. "Still profitable" is not the test; "is the NEXT unit profitable" is.

Verify from both sides: the last unit produced must add profit (MC below MR) and the next one must subtract it (MC above MR). If time allows, confirm with the brute-force profit column - total revenue minus total cost at each output - which must peak at the same output the marginal rule selected. Two independent methods agreeing is proof, not luck. In Grade 12, perfect and imperfect market questions interrogate exactly this table - only the shape of the revenue side changes.

economics.demand_and_supply.recap:
Demand is the quantity buyers are willing AND able to buy at each price; supply is what producers are willing and able to offer. The law of demand: price up, quantity demanded down - so the demand curve slopes downward. The law of supply: price up, quantity supplied up, because price is the producer's reward - so the supply curve slopes upward. Convention: price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal.

The distinction that decides marks: movement along a curve versus a shift of the whole curve. Ask one question - did the good's OWN price cause the change? If yes, slide along the existing curve (a change in quantity demanded or supplied). If anything else changed, the whole curve shifts. Demand shifters: income, tastes, prices of substitutes and complements, population. Supply shifters: input costs, technology, taxes and subsidies, number of producers, and natural conditions like weather.

Where the curves cross is equilibrium: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied and the market clears. No other price can last. Above equilibrium, supply outruns demand - a surplus - and unsold stock pushes the price down. Below equilibrium, demand outruns supply - a shortage - and competing buyers bid the price up. The market settles at equilibrium through these forces alone; nobody sets the price.

Worked diagnosis - the drought question. A drought halves the maize harvest; consumer income is unchanged. Which side is hit? The farms: supply. Did the maize price cause it? No, weather did: shift the whole supply curve, leftward, because less is offered at every price. Demand stays put - income is unchanged. At the old price there is now a shortage; buyers bid the price up; as it rises, some buyers cut back (a movement along the demand curve) until the shortage disappears. New equilibrium: higher price, smaller quantity traded.

Answer method: labelled axes, both curves, original equilibrium marked with dotted lines, the shifted curve with an arrow, new equilibrium read off, then two sentences explaining the shortage or surplus that moved the price. The diagram shows what happened; the words earn the reasoning marks.

economics.graphing_from_tables.recap:
A demand and supply schedule is a table listing, for each price, the quantity buyers would demand and the quantity sellers would supply. Turning it into a graph makes it an answer machine - but only if it is built properly.

Read the table before drawing. The demand column should fall as price rises (law of demand - a downward curve coming) and the supply column should rise (law of supply - upward curve). Spot the row where the two columns are equal: that row is the equilibrium, and your curves must cross exactly there. Note the ranges of price and quantity - they decide your axis scales.

Build the axes by convention: price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal - always, even though it feels backwards. Choose even scales, where equal distances mean equal amounts; an uneven scale bends the curves and corrupts every reading afterwards. Label both axes with units and give the graph a heading - markers award these directly.

Plot one point per table row: go up to the price, across to the quantity, mark. Join the demand points into a smooth curve labelled D, and the supply points into S on the same axes. Their intersection is the equilibrium: read its price and quantity off the axes with dotted lines and label the point E. Confirm against the table - the crossing must land on the row where the columns match; if it does not, a point is misplotted or a scale is uneven.

Reading gaps is the exam skill. For excess supply at a given price: run a horizontal line at that price; where it cuts the demand curve, read quantity demanded; where it cuts the supply curve, read quantity supplied; subtract. Both readings must come from the same price - the commonest error is mixing prices. A price above equilibrium always shows supply exceeding demand (a surplus, pushing price down); below equilibrium, demand exceeds supply (a shortage, pulling price up).

Verification habit: every point checked against its row, slopes matching the laws, intersection matching the equal row, and any surplus or shortage computed as a subtraction of two same-price readings.

exit_check.prompt: Your curves cross at a price where the table's two columns are NOT equal. This means:
options: A point is misplotted or a scale is uneven - recheck against the table

exit_check.prompt: Why must an axis use even steps?
options: Uneven steps bend the curves and make every reading unreliable
It only matters for the supply curve

exit_check.prompt: The most common error when reading excess supply off a graph is:
options: Taking the two quantity readings at different prices

economics.monetary_and_fiscal_policy.example_problem: Inflation is above the target band. State the instrument the SARB is most likely to use and its transmission to spending; contrast with two fiscal-policy instruments the finance minister controls, and classify each as expansionary or contractionary.

covered_by.subtopic: Central banking: basic functions, monetary policy

diagnostic.prompt: Inflation is above the 3-6% target band. The SARB's most likely response is to:
'The Minister of Finance raises the repo rate.' What is wrong with this statement?
options: The repo rate is controlled by the SARB, not the minister

economics.monetary_and_fiscal_policy.recap:
Two policies steer the economy, driven by two different hands. Monetary policy belongs to the South African Reserve Bank - independent of government, mandated to protect the currency's value, in practice keeping inflation inside the 3 to 6 percent target band. Its headline instrument is the repo rate. Fiscal policy belongs to the government, announced by the Minister of Finance in the Budget; its instruments are government spending and taxation. The test for any instrument: whose hand is on it? Reserve Bank - monetary. The Budget - fiscal.

The repo rate is what commercial banks pay to borrow from the SARB, and its effects travel a chain. Repo up: banks' funding costs rise; banks raise their prime lending rate; home loans, car finance and credit become dearer; households and firms cut back on borrowing and spending; total demand slows, and with less money chasing goods, the pressure on prices eases. That is contractionary monetary policy. The honest trade-off: the same medicine cools growth and can cost jobs in the short run. The reverse - cutting the repo rate - cheapens credit and stimulates spending: expansionary.

Fiscal policy fights inflation from the demand side too: restrain government spending (fewer projects, tighter budgets) and/or raise taxes (less disposable income, dearer spending) - both contractionary. In a recession, the gears reverse: more spending and tax cuts pump demand in - expansionary. Classify any move by asking whether it puts spending power into the economy (expansionary) or withdraws it (contractionary).

The comparison exams love: monetary policy is fast but blunt - the Monetary Policy Committee meets every two months, and the repo rate hits every borrower in the country indiscriminately. Fiscal policy is slower - the Budget is annual and political - but can be aimed at specific sectors, taxes or programmes. The two work best pulling together: if the SARB tightens while government spends freely, the policies fight each other and the SARB must tighten harder.

Answer method: name the problem (inflation or recession), name the driver, name the instrument, state the direction and classification, then walk the transmission chain step by step to prices. Wrong-hand statements - a minister moving the repo rate - are themselves the error to spot.

exit_check.prompt: Which chain correctly orders the transmission of a repo rate increase?
options: Repo up → prime up → loans dearer → spending slows → price pressure eases
Repo up → taxes up → spending up → inflation up
Repo up → prime down → borrowing rises → inflation falls
Repo up → exports rise → inflation falls

exit_check.prompt: A VAT increase is classified as:
options: Contractionary fiscal policy - it withdraws spending power

exit_check.prompt: Monetary policy versus fiscal policy is best summarised as:
options: Fast but blunt versus slower but targeted
Both identical in speed and reach

geography.contour_reading.subtopic: 1:50 000 topographic maps: natural and constructed features, height clues, contour patterns (river valleys, hills, mountains, ridges, spurs)
geography.contour_reading.name: Reading contour lines
geography.contour_reading.example_problem: On a 1:50 000 extract with a 20 m contour interval, identify the river valley, the steepest slope and the spot height, and explain how contour spacing shows gradient.
geography.contour_reading.prior_knowledge: Map symbols and height representation from Gr 8-9 mapwork

importance.summary: Mapwork is Question 3 on BOTH Geography papers, every year: 30/150 per paper in Gr 11 and Gr 12 (map skills & calculations 10, map interpretation 12, GIS 8) - contour reading is the entry point.

diagnostic.prompt: Contour lines drawn very close together indicate:
options: A steep slope - the fixed height gain happens over a short horizontal distance

diagnostic.prompt: In a river valley, the V-shaped bends in the contour lines point:
options: Uphill, toward the higher ground upstream

geography.contour_reading.recap:
A contour line joins all points of equal height above sea level - walk along one and you neither climb nor descend. On a 1:50 000 topographic sheet the contour interval is typically 20 m: each line is 20 m higher or lower than its neighbours. Check the interval in the key before anything else. Three rules police every map: contours never cross (a point cannot have two heights), never simply end (they close into loops or run off the sheet), and every fourth or fifth line is a thicker, labelled index contour - your anchor for counting. A point between the 820 and 840 lines lies between those heights; a spot height (a dot with a number, like 913) pins a summit's exact altitude, which contours alone cannot give.

Spacing is gradient. Between neighbouring contours the land always rises the fixed interval; what varies is the horizontal distance walked to gain it. Lines far apart: the rise is spread over a long walk - gentle. Lines crowded: the same rise over a short distance - steep. Lines almost touching: a cliff. Even spacing means a uniform slope; wide-at-top, close-at-bottom is concave; close-at-top, wide-at-bottom is convex. To justify "steepest slope" in an exam, quote the evidence: the contours are closest together here, so the land rises 20 m over the shortest horizontal distance.

Valleys and spurs are the classic confusion pair, both showing bent contours. A valley's contours bend in a V pointing UPHILL, toward the upstream high ground - the line must detour up the low ground to keep its height - and a river often runs through it. A spur is high ground jutting between valleys: its bulge points DOWNHILL and never carries a river. When in doubt, read the heights on either side and ask which way is up. Confirm any river's direction two ways: the Vs point upstream, and the contour values crossing the river must decrease downstream - water never flows uphill.

Other signatures: closed rings with rising values - a hill; a stretched high band - a ridge; the dip between two summits - a saddle; almost no contours - a plain. Method for any question: read the interval, find the index contours, identify features by pattern, confirm with the printed heights, and answer by quoting spacing and values as evidence.

exit_check.prompt: Why can two contour lines never cross?
options: A single point cannot have two different heights
It would make the map untidy
Rivers would have nowhere to flow

exit_check.prompt: Contours crossing a river read 840, 820, 800 in the direction you trace it. You are tracing:
options: Downstream - heights must decrease in the direction of flow

exit_check.prompt: A bulge of contours pointing downhill, with no river, is a:
options: Spur - high ground jutting out between valleys

exit_check.prompt: What extra information does a spot height give that contours cannot?
options: The exact altitude of a point, not just a between-lines range

geography.gradient_calculation.subject: Geography
geography.gradient_calculation.name: Gradient calculation
geography.gradient_calculation.example_problem: Calculate the average gradient between trig beacon 251 (1 200 m) and a spot height of 900 m that are 4,5 km apart on a 1:50 000 topographic map.
geography.gradient_calculation.prior_knowledge: Student can read contour lines and convert between map units

importance.summary: A named mapwork calculation: part of Question 3's map skills and calculations (10 of the 30 mapwork marks on each paper) and required for fluvial/geomorphology cross-section work.

diagnostic.prompt: Trig beacon 251 stands at 1 200 m and a spot height at 900 m; the points are 4,5 km apart. The average gradient is:
Which slope is steeper?

geography.gradient_calculation.recap:
Gradient turns the contour-spacing impression of steepness into an exact number. The formula: gradient = vertical interval ÷ horizontal equivalent (VI over HE, rise over run), expressed as a ratio 1 : x, meaning the land rises 1 m vertically for every x metres travelled horizontally. Interpretation rule that catches many candidates: the LARGER the number after the colon, the GENTLER the slope - 1 : 15 is far steeper than 1 : 150, because the metre of climb is diluted over more walking.

Harvest the two ingredients from the map. VI is the height difference: higher point minus lower point, taken from the best height sources available - trig beacons and spot heights give exact surveyed values, contours give ranges. HE is the horizontal distance between the points; if not given, measure the map distance and convert with the scale (on 1:50 000, centimetres × 50 000, then down the unit ladder). The non-negotiable step: both ingredients must be in the SAME units before dividing - convert kilometres to metres. Mixed units are the deadliest error in this calculation.

Worked example, exam layout. Beacon at 1 200 m, spot height at 900 m, 4,5 km apart. Line one, formula: gradient = VI ÷ HE. Line two, substitution in matching units: 300 m ÷ 4 500 m. Line three, simplify by dividing both by the numerator: 4 500 ÷ 300 = 15. Line four, answer in ratio form: 1 : 15 - and only this form collects the final mark; a decimal or unsimplified fraction usually does not. Add one interpretation sentence: the land rises 1 m for every 15 m travelled - noticeably steep, too steep for a railway.

It is an AVERAGE gradient because the real land may dip and climb between the points; the ratio smears the total rise evenly over the total distance - a straight-line summary of a possibly bumpy reality.

Three closing checks: sense (is the steepness plausible for land - a wild x signals a unit slip), reverse arithmetic (15 × 300 = 4 500), and order (the vertical 1 leads the ratio; for ordinary land x should exceed 1, since you walk further than you climb).

exit_check.prompt: Why must 4,5 km become 4 500 m before dividing?
options: The ratio only has meaning when VI and HE are in the same units
Kilometres are not allowed in Geography

exit_check.prompt: A learner reports the answer as 15 : 1. The error is:
options: An inverted ratio - the vertical 1 m of climb must lead

exit_check.prompt: Why is the result called an AVERAGE gradient?
options: The total rise is spread evenly over the total distance, ignoring dips and climbs between the points
The map scale is an average

diagnostic.prompt: Two points are 8,6 cm apart on a 1:50 000 map. The real distance is:
On a 1:50 000 sheet, one centimetre of map represents:

geography.map_scale_and_distance.recap:
The ratio scale 1:50 000 means one unit of any length on the map represents 50 000 of the same units on the ground. It is unitless - measure in centimetres and multiply by 50 000, and the answer is in centimetres of real ground. Feel the size: 50 000 cm is 500 m, so every map centimetre is half a kilometre; two centimetres, one kilometre.

The standard calculation, four lines. One: measure (or receive) the map distance - point-centre to point-centre, to the nearest millimetre; at this scale each millimetre of sloppiness is 50 m of ground. Two: multiply by the scale factor - 8,6 cm × 50 000 = 430 000 cm. Three: walk the metric ladder - divide by 100 for metres (4 300 m), divide by 1 000 for kilometres (4,3 km). Four: state the answer WITH its unit, in the unit the question demands. The ladder chant: centi to metres, divide by a hundred; metres to kays, divide by a thousand.

Curved distances - a winding road or river - defeat a rigid ruler: lay a string or paper-strip edge along the bends, mark the end, straighten it against the ruler, and read the total map distance; the arithmetic afterwards is identical. Memos accept a small range on curved measurements, so press the string into every bend rather than cutting corners.

Different scale, same machine: on a 1:10 000 orthophoto, multiply by 10 000 instead - 8,6 cm is only 0,86 km. Never assume the scale; read it off the sheet, especially when a question moves between the topographic map and the orthophoto. And remember which is the LARGER scale: 1:10 000, because one ten-thousandth is the bigger fraction - larger scale, smaller area, more detail. The reverse question runs the machine backwards: real distance to map distance means convert to centimetres, then DIVIDE by the scale factor - 4,3 km = 430 000 cm ÷ 50 000 = 8,6 cm.

The sense check that saves matrics: about 10 cm on a 1:50 000 sheet is 5 km. If 8,6 cm produces 43 km or 0,43 km, a decimal slipped on the ladder. Convert, then ask whether you could walk the answer in an afternoon.

exit_check.prompt: The metric ladder from centimetres to kilometres runs:
To measure distance along a winding river on the map, you should:
options: Lay string or a paper strip along the bends, straighten it, and read against a ruler

exit_check.prompt: Which map has the larger scale, and what does that mean?
options: 1:10 000 - a bigger fraction, showing a smaller area in more detail

exit_check.prompt: The real distance is 4,3 km. On a 1:50 000 map the points are apart by:
options: 8,6 cm - convert to 430 000 cm and divide by 50 000

diagnostic.prompt: A station model shows temperature 18 °C and dew point 16 °C. The small gap tells you:
options: The air is nearly saturated - humid, with cloud or rain close at hand
The station is at high altitude

diagnostic.prompt: A wind shaft flies into the station circle from the north-west with two full feathers. The wind is:
options: Blowing toward the north-west at 10 knots

geography.synoptic_map_reading.recap:
A synoptic chart is a snapshot of the atmosphere at one moment. Isobars join places of equal pressure (in hPa) and work like contour lines for the atmosphere: around an H (high) pressure rises to the centre, around an L (low) it falls. The weather logic: in a high, air sinks, warms and dries - clear, settled weather; in a low, air rises, cools and condenses - cloud and rain. Sink = clear, rise = rain. Closely packed isobars mean a steep pressure gradient and strong winds.

Each station circle compresses a full report. The circle's shading gives cloud cover in eighths (oktas) - six-eighths shaded means three-quarters of the sky is cloudy. Top-left of the circle: air temperature. Below it: dew point - the temperature at which the air would saturate. Never read the dew point alone; read the GAP between it and the air temperature. A small gap (18 °C against 16 °C) means the air needs to cool only slightly to condense - humid, cloud and rain nearby. A wide gap means dry air. Wind is a shaft with feathers: the shaft flies INTO the circle from the direction the wind comes FROM (winds are always named for their origin), and feathers count speed - a full feather 10 knots, a half feather 5.

South Africa's weather-maker is the cold front - a bold line of triangles, the triangles pointing in the direction of movement, sweeping from south-west to north-east ahead of a low passing south of the country. Confirm a front with evidence on both sides. Ahead of it: warm, humid north-westerly flow with thickening cloud - the classic pre-frontal station. At the line: dense cold air wedges under the warm air and forces it violently upward, building cumulonimbus and the heaviest weather. Behind it: temperature drops sharply, the wind swings from north-westerly to south-westerly, pressure rises as the next high builds in, and showery weather clears. Cold, showery, clearing - the post-frontal trio. The NW-to-SW wind swing is often the single clearest sign a front has passed a station.

Method: find the pressure cells, read isobar spacing for wind, decode the station models, locate fronts by symbol and confirm with the air masses on either side - then answer in observations, quoting the numbers and directions.

exit_check.prompt: Why does a high-pressure cell generally bring clear weather?
options: Sinking air warms and dries as it descends

exit_check.prompt: Behind a South African cold front, the weather is typically:
options: Colder, south-westerly winds, rising pressure, showers then clearing

exit_check.prompt: On the chart, a cold front is drawn as:
options: A line with triangles pointing in its direction of movement

maths.factorisation_techniques.subject: Maths
maths.factorisation_techniques.subtopic: Factorisation: trinomials, grouping in pairs, sum and difference of two cubes
maths.factorisation_techniques.name: Factorisation techniques
maths.factorisation_techniques.example_problem: Factorise fully: 6x^2 - 7x - 3; x^3 + 8; and 2ax + 2ay - bx - by (grouping in pairs).

importance.summary: Feeds the Algebra section every year (30/100 Gr 10, 45/150 Gr 11, 25/150 Gr 12 on Paper 1) AND Gr 12 Differential Calculus (35/150), where the factor theorem is applied to cubics.

covered_by.subtopic: Factorisation: trinomials, grouping in pairs, sum and difference of two cubes

diagnostic.prompt: Factorised fully, 6x² − 7x − 3 equals:
Factorised fully, x³ + 8 equals:

maths.factorisation_techniques.recap:
Factorising reverses expanding: it breaks an expression into the brackets whose product it is. Run the same decision tree every time. First, always: take out any common factor across all terms. Then count the terms - the count picks the tool. Two terms: difference of squares, or sum/difference of cubes. Three terms: the trinomial method. Four terms: grouping in pairs. Finally, check every bracket in your answer for further factorising - "fully" is a contract.

Trinomials ax² + bx + c: hunt two numbers whose product is a × c and whose sum is b. For 6x² − 7x − 3: product 6 × (−3) = −18, sum −7. Read the signs first - negative product means opposite signs; negative sum means the bigger number is negative. The pair is −9 and +2. Split the middle term: 6x² − 9x + 2x − 3; group in pairs: 3x(2x − 3) + 1(2x − 3); the matching brackets are the built-in check - if they differ, the split or a sign is wrong. Factor the bracket out: (2x − 3)(3x + 1).

Cubes: recognise perfect cubes (1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216; x³; y⁶). The identities share one pattern - a short bracket of the two cube roots, and a long bracket built square-the-first, multiply-the-pair, square-the-last - with signs by SOAP: Same as the original, Opposite for the middle term, Always Positive last. So x³ + 8 = (x + 2)(x² − 2x + 4). The middle term is a × b (2x), not a square (never 4x), and the long bracket NEVER factorises further - stopping there is correct.

Grouping in pairs, for four terms: 2ax + 2ay − bx − by. Pair as they stand, factor each pair - and when a pair leads with a minus, take out a NEGATIVE factor so the bracket's signs flip into a match: 2a(x + y) − b(x + y). Then factor out the common bracket: (x + y)(2a − b). If pairs share nothing, rearrange kin together first.

Verify everything the same way: expand your answer and confirm the original returns. Thirty seconds, and the answer is proven rather than hoped.

exit_check.prompt: For 6x² − 7x − 3, the split numbers must satisfy:
In SOAP for the cubes identities, the letters give:
options: Same, Opposite, Always Positive - the three signs

exit_check.prompt: Grouping −bx − by requires factoring out:
The reliable check for any factorisation is:
options: Expand the answer and confirm the original expression returns

maths.laws_of_exponents.subtopic: Use exponent laws to simplify expressions and solve equations (rational exponents)
maths.laws_of_exponents.name: Laws of exponents
maths.laws_of_exponents.prior_knowledge: Gr 9 exponent laws for integer exponents

importance.summary: Part of the Algebra section on every Paper 1: 30/100 in Gr 10, 45/150 in Gr 11, 25/150 in Gr 12 - and assumed inside functions and finance work.

covered_by.subtopic: Use exponent laws to simplify expressions and solve equations (rational exponents)

diagnostic.prompt: Simplified fully, (2x³y)² × 4x⁻² ÷ (8xy²) equals:
The solution of 3^(x+1) = 27 is:

maths.laws_of_exponents.recap:
An exponent counts repeated multiplication, and every law follows from that. Multiplying powers of the same base: ADD the exponents (x³ × x² = x⁵ - five x's strung together). Dividing: SUBTRACT (x⁵ ÷ x² = x³ - two x's cancel). A power on a power: MULTIPLY ((x³)² = x⁶). A bracket raised to a power gives that power to EVERY factor inside: (2xy)² = 4x²y² - the coefficient is squared too; leaving the 2 unsquared is the most common bracket error. Two consequences complete the kit: anything nonzero to the power zero is 1 (because x³ ÷ x³ is both 1 and x⁰), and a negative exponent means reciprocal - x⁻² = 1/x² - a POSITION instruction (move across the fraction line), never a negative number: 4x⁻² is 4/x², not −4x².

Simplifying strategy: clear bracket powers first, then gather like bases and handle each base on its own - numbers with numbers, x's with x's, y's with y's; the laws never combine different bases (x² × y³ is not (xy)⁵). Worked: (2x³y)² × 4x⁻² ÷ (8xy²). Bracket first: 4x⁶y². Multiply by 4x⁻²: coefficients 16, x-exponents 6 + (−2) = 4, giving 16x⁴y². Divide by 8xy²: coefficients 16 ÷ 8 = 2; x: 4 − 1 = 3; y: 2 − 2 = 0, so the y's vanish. Answer: 2x³. Check with a quick substitution (x = 1, y = 1 in original and answer; x = 2 if time allows, since 1 hides exponent slips).

Exponential equations put the unknown in the exponent, and one move solves them: make the bases match. If two powers of the same positive base (not 1) are equal, their exponents must be equal. 3^(x+1) = 27: rewrite 27 as 3³, so x + 1 = 3 and x = 2. The same move handles the variations: right side 1 means 3⁰ (x = −1); right side 1/27 means 3⁻³ (x = −4). Do not divide both sides by 3 hoping to peel the exponent - by the subtraction law that only lowers it by one. Match the bases, equate the exponents, solve, substitute back to confirm.

exit_check.prompt: (2x³y)² expands to:
4x⁻² written with positive exponents is:
The key move for solving 3^(x+1) = 27 is:
options: Rewrite 27 as 3³ so both sides share a base, then equate exponents

exit_check.prompt: y² divided by y² in a simplification gives:
options: y⁰ = 1 - the y's vanish from the answer

diagnostic.prompt: Without a calculator, sin 60° × cos 30° − tan 45° equals:
In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is 13 and the side opposite angle x is 5. Then x equals:

maths.trig_ratios.recap:
In a right-angled triangle, pick an acute angle and the sides take names relative to IT: the hypotenuse (longest, opposite the right angle - never changes), the opposite (facing your angle), and the adjacent (the angle's other arm). The ratios: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent - SOH CAH TOA. These ratios are properties of the angle, not the triangle: similar triangles keep them identical at any size, which is why sin 30° is a fixed number of the universe. Label AFTER choosing your angle - switch to the other acute angle and opposite and adjacent swap places.

The special-angle values come from two rebuildable triangles, not memory. Halve an equilateral triangle of side 2: hypotenuse 2, base 1, height √3 - giving sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √3, and from the top angle sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3. A right-angled isosceles triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse √2: sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2, tan 45° = 1. Evaluate exactly, keeping surds: sin 60° × cos 30° = (√3/2)(√3/2) = 3/4; minus tan 45° = 1 gives −1/4. Exact fractions, never rounded decimals, when the question says no calculator.

Choosing the ratio is the real skill: mark the angle, label the three sides relative to it, circle the two sides that are known or wanted, and pick the ratio whose letters match - opposite and hypotenuse: sine; adjacent and hypotenuse: cosine; opposite and adjacent: tangent.

Finding an angle runs the machine in reverse. Hypotenuse 13, opposite 5: sin x = 5/13, so x = sin⁻¹(5/13) ≈ 22,6° (shift-sin on the calculator, in DEGREE mode - check for the D; radian mode turns sin 30° into −0,988 and poisons everything). Direction decides the button: angle known, side wanted - plain function; sides known, angle wanted - inverse. Sense-check: 5/13 is less than 1/2 and sin 30° = 1/2, so the angle must be under 30° - and in the 5-12-13 triangle the other acute angle, sin⁻¹(12/13) ≈ 67,4°, completes 90° exactly.

exit_check.prompt: Which side of a right-angled triangle never changes its label?
options: The hypotenuse - always opposite the right angle

exit_check.prompt: sin 60° equals:
You know the opposite (5) and adjacent (12) sides and want the angle. Use:
A calculator giving sin 30° = −0,988 most likely means:
options: It is in radian mode instead of degree mode

maths_literacy.graph_interpretation.example_problem: From a line graph of two electricity tariff options, read the break-even usage, state which option is cheaper for 450 kWh, and describe what the steeper gradient means in rands per kWh.

importance.summary: Tariff-comparison and break-even questions in Finance (Q2, Paper 1) and the integration questions (Q4-5 on both papers) are asked through graphs.

covered_by.subtopic: Interpreting tables and graphs: zero, minimum, maximum and missing values; write a story from a graph and draw a graph from a story

diagnostic.prompt: Option A: R2,00 per kWh, no fixed charge. Option B: R150 fixed + R1,50 per kWh. For 450 kWh, which is cheaper?
options: Option B at R825, beating Option A's R900 by R75

diagnostic.prompt: A cost line starts at R150 on the vertical axis. That intercept represents:
options: The fixed charge, paid even at zero usage

maths_literacy.graph_interpretation.recap:
A cost line on a money graph tells you a tariff's whole structure in two readings. The vertical intercept - where the line starts at zero usage - is the FIXED CHARGE: an option with no fixed charge starts at the origin; an option with a R150 monthly fee starts at R150. The gradient - how fast the line climbs - is the PRICE PER UNIT: a line rising R2,00 for every kilowatt-hour is steeper than one rising R1,50, because each unit costs more. Steeper always means more expensive per unit. You can measure a gradient off any line: pick two easy points, divide the rise in rand by the run in units.

Where two options' lines cross is the BREAK-EVEN point: the usage at which both cost exactly the same. Read it by tracing down to the usage axis and across to the cost axis, then verify by calculation - both tariffs computed at that usage must give the same rand amount. With Option A at R2,00 per kWh and Option B at R150 plus R1,50 per kWh, break-even is 300 kWh, where both cost R600.

Break-even splits the graph into decision zones. Left of the crossing (low usage), the no-fixed-charge option's line runs lower: light users should not pay an entrance fee for a per-unit discount they barely use. Right of the crossing (high usage), the fixed-charge option dips underneath: the 50c saving on every unit eventually outweighs the R150 fee. At any usage, the LOWEST line at that point is the cheapest option - run a finger up from the usage value and the first line struck wins.

For a specific comparison, always finish with the arithmetic and state the difference: at 450 kWh, Option A costs 450 × R2,00 = R900; Option B costs R150 + 450 × R1,50 = R825; B is cheaper by R75. Comparison answers earn full marks when they show both totals and the saving, not just the winner's name. Close with a sense check: heavy users benefiting from cheap units, and zero usage costing R0 on one option but R150 on the other, both match what the tariffs say in words.

exit_check.prompt: On a tariff graph, the gradient of a cost line represents:
options: The price per unit - how much the bill climbs per extra unit used

exit_check.prompt: At the break-even usage:
options: Both options cost exactly the same
The cheaper option is always the steeper line

exit_check.prompt: For any usage level, the cheapest option is found by:
options: Reading which line is lowest at that usage
Choosing the line with the higher intercept

maths_literacy.percentage_calculations.subject: Mathematical Literacy
maths_literacy.percentage_calculations.subtopic: Rounding (to decimal places, nearest whole, up or down); ratios; rates (meaning, types, calculations); direct and inverse proportion; percentages incl. increase and decrease
maths_literacy.percentage_calculations.name: Percentage calculations
maths_literacy.percentage_calculations.example_problem: A jacket priced at R850 is discounted by 15%, then 15% VAT is added to the discounted price. Calculate the final price, and the single percentage change from the original price.
maths_literacy.percentage_calculations.prior_knowledge: Fractions and decimals; multiplication and division

importance.summary: Finance is Question 2 on every Paper 1 (Gr 10 75 marks -> Gr 11 100 -> Gr 12 150), and percentages run through VAT, interest, inflation and tariff work; Q1's 20% level-1 marks lean on it too.

covered_by.subtopic: Rounding (to decimal places, nearest whole, up or down); ratios; rates (meaning, types, calculations); direct and inverse proportion; percentages incl. increase and decrease

diagnostic.prompt: A jacket priced at R850 is discounted by 15%, then 15% VAT is added to the discounted price. The final price is:
A price of R830,88 INCLUDES 15% VAT. The price before VAT is found by:

maths_literacy.percentage_calculations.recap:
A percentage is a fraction out of 100: 15% is 0,15. Percentage OF an amount: multiply - 15% of R850 is 0,15 × 850 = R127,50.

The upgrade that handles everything else is the single multiplier. A decrease of 15% leaves 85% of the amount: multiply by 0,85 in one step. An increase of 15% gives 115%: multiply by 1,15. Decrease: one MINUS the decimal; increase: one PLUS the decimal. The multiplier is not a trick - "take off 15%" and "keep 85%" are the same sentence.

Chained changes multiply, and each step acts on the RESULT of the previous step, never on the original. The jacket: R850 × 0,85 = R722,50 after the discount; then VAT on the discounted price: R722,50 × 1,15 = R830,88 (rounded to the cent). The famous trap: minus 15% then plus 15% does NOT return to R850. The discount removed 15% of R850 (R127,50), but the VAT added back 15% of the smaller R722,50 (R108,38) - equal rates on unequal bases are unequal amounts of money. Down-then-up by the same rate always lands slightly below the start.

The combined effect of a chain is the product of the multipliers: 0,85 × 1,15 = 0,9775, meaning the final price is 97,75% of the original - an overall 2,25% DECREASE, in one multiplication. Confirm with the direct formula for percentage change: change ÷ ORIGINAL × 100. The original is always the denominator - the reference point is where you started - so (850 − 830,88) ÷ 850 × 100 = 2,25%.

Reverse percentages undo a change. A price tag of R830,88 INCLUDING 15% VAT: the tag equals the pre-VAT price times 1,15, so divide - 830,88 ÷ 1,15 = R722,50. Subtracting 15% instead is wrong because it takes 15% of the larger final price, not of the smaller base the VAT was actually charged on. To undo any multiplier, divide by it.

The five moves: percentage of - decimal times amount; increase or decrease - one multiplier; chains - multiply the multipliers, each on the previous result; percentage change - difference over original times 100; reverse - divide by the multiplier. Every VAT, discount, interest, inflation and tariff question is one of these five.

exit_check.prompt: The single multiplier for a 15% decrease is:
Why do −15% then +15% not cancel out?
options: The increase acts on a smaller base than the decrease removed from
VAT is calculated by SARS differently

exit_check.prompt: In the percentage change formula, the denominator is always:
A combined multiplier of 0,9775 across a chain of changes means:

maths_literacy.substitution_in_formulae.subject: Mathematical Literacy
maths_literacy.substitution_in_formulae.name: Substitution into formulae
maths_literacy.substitution_in_formulae.example_problem: Using cost = R450 + R12,50 x km, calculate the cost of a 340 km trip; then find how many kilometres R1 200 buys.

importance.summary: Measurement is Question 3 on every Paper 2, and tariff/cost formulas in Finance (Q2, Paper 1) are substitution work - it earns marks on both papers every year.

diagnostic.prompt: Using cost = R450 + R12,50 × km, a 340 km trip costs:
With the same formula, how many kilometres does R1 200 buy?

maths_literacy.substitution_in_formulae.recap:
A formula is a machine: numbers in, answer out. Read it as a story before calculating. In cost = R450 + R12,50 × km, the R450 stands alone - the fixed charge, owed before any driving; the R12,50 is glued to the kilometres - the rate, growing with usage. Fixed plus rate-times-usage is the skeleton of tariffs, contracts, call-out fees and deliveries alike.

Forward substitution: the input is known, the output wanted. Write the formula, then the substitution line - both usually earn their own marks - then compute respecting the order of operations: multiplication BEFORE addition, always. For 340 km: 12,50 × 340 = 4 250 first, then + 450 gives R4 700. Adding first (450 + 12,50, then × 340) produces the R157 250 disaster - a hire bill that buys the car. Sense-check the size and state the unit.

Reverse substitution: the output is known, the input wanted. Substitute what you know, then unwind with inverse operations in reverse order - like taking off shoes before socks. The money logic gives the order for free: the budget pays the fixed fee at the door first, and only the remainder buys usage. R1 200 = 450 + 12,50 × km: subtract the fixed charge (1 200 − 450 = 750 left for driving), then divide by the rate (750 ÷ 12,50 = 60 km). The classic error divides the whole budget by the rate (1 200 ÷ 12,50 = 96 km, wrong) - the R450 never bought a single kilometre and must be peeled off first.

Reverse answers come with a free proof: run the machine forwards with your answer. 450 + 12,50 × 60 = 1 200 - exactly the budget, so 60 km is verified, not hoped.

The six steps for any formula: write it down unchanged; identify the known and wanted variables; substitute, converting units first if the formula's units differ from the question's; compute forwards with the order of operations, or unwind backwards fixed-part-first; state the answer with its unit; verify - sense-check the size, and substitute reverse answers back. The exam prints the formula for you; careful feeding and patient unwinding are the whole skill.

exit_check.prompt: In cost = R450 + R12,50 × km, which must be computed first when substituting km = 340?
In the reverse question, why is dividing the whole R1 200 by R12,50 wrong?
options: R450 of the budget pays the fixed fee and buys no distance - remove it before dividing

exit_check.prompt: How is a reverse answer of 60 km verified?

physical_sciences.equations_of_motion.subject: Physical Sciences
physical_sciences.equations_of_motion.subtopic: Equations of motion in the horizontal plane; vehicle safety and stopping distance
physical_sciences.equations_of_motion.name: Equations of motion
physical_sciences.equations_of_motion.example_problem: A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 25 m/s over 300 m. Choose the correct equation of motion, calculate the acceleration, and then the time taken.

importance.summary: Mechanics is the biggest Gr 12 Paper 1 section (65/150); momentum & impulse, vertical projectile motion and work-energy-power all build directly on these equations.

covered_by.topic: MECHANICS: Instantaneous speed and velocity and the equations of motion
covered_by.subtopic: Equations of motion in the horizontal plane; vehicle safety and stopping distance

diagnostic.prompt: A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 25 m/s over 300 m. Its acceleration is:
options: 0,875 m/s² in the direction of motion

diagnostic.prompt: A problem gives vi, vf and Δx and asks for a. Which equation fits immediately?
options: vf² = vi² + 2aΔx - the one with no time in it

physical_sciences.equations_of_motion.recap:
The equations of motion describe straight-line movement with UNIFORM (constant) acceleration - the word "uniformly" in a problem is your licence to use them at all. Five quantities star in every problem: initial velocity vi, final velocity vf, acceleration a, time Δt, and displacement Δx.

Four equations, each missing exactly one quantity: vf = vi + aΔt (no displacement); Δx = viΔt + ½aΔt² (no final velocity); vf² = vi² + 2aΔx (no time); Δx = (vi + vf)/2 × Δt (no acceleration - the average-velocity equation). That missing character is the whole secret of choosing. Every problem gives three quantities and wants a fourth; the fifth - neither given nor wanted - is absent, and the right equation is the one that EXCLUDES it. Never grab the first equation you remember: match the hole to the absent quantity.

Method: first list Given, Wanted and Absent formally, converting units as you list - km/h becomes m/s by dividing by 3,6 (90 km/h = 25 m/s), and skipping this poisons every later step. Then choose by the absent character, substitute with units, solve, and state vector answers with a direction.

Worked: a car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 25 m/s over 300 m. Given vi, vf, Δx; wanted a; absent: time - so vf² = vi² + 2aΔx. Substitute: 625 = 100 + 600a (write the squares out immediately - 25² is 625, not 25). Solve: a = 525/600 = 0,875 m/s² in the direction of motion. For the time: vf = vi + aΔt gives 15 = 0,875Δt, so Δt = 17,14 s.

Verify by a second road wherever possible: Δx = (vi + vf)/2 × Δt uses only ORIGINAL data - the average of 10 and 25 is 17,5, and 300 ÷ 17,5 = 17,14 s again. Two independent routes agreeing proves both answers; a wrong acceleration could not have hidden. Final habits: sense-check size and sign (a braking car has negative a in your chosen positive direction - keep vector signs consistent), and remember these same equations return in matric as vertical projectile motion with a = 9,8 m/s² downward.

exit_check.prompt: The equations of motion may only be used when:
90 km/h converted for use in the equations is:
Why is checking the time with Δx = (vi + vf)/2 × Δt such a strong verification?
options: It uses only original given data, so an error in the calculated acceleration cannot hide
It always gives a rounder number

physical_sciences.force_and_free_body_di.subject: Physical Sciences
physical_sciences.force_and_free_body_di.subtopic: Force diagrams and free-body diagrams; resolving weight on an inclined plane
physical_sciences.force_and_free_body_di.name: Force diagrams and free-body diagrams
physical_sciences.force_and_free_body_di.example_problem: A 5 kg box is pulled at constant velocity across a rough floor by a rope at 30 degrees. Draw the free-body diagram naming weight, normal force, applied force and friction.
physical_sciences.force_and_free_body_di.prior_knowledge: Types of forces; vectors and scalars

importance.summary: The working tool of the Mechanics section (65/150 of the Gr 12 Paper 1): Newton's laws and work-energy questions start with a correct free-body diagram.

covered_by.subtopic: Force diagrams and free-body diagrams; resolving weight on an inclined plane

diagnostic.prompt: A 5 kg box is pulled at constant velocity across a rough floor by a rope at 30° above the horizontal. The forces on the box are:
options: Weight, normal force, applied force along the rope, friction backward
Weight, normal force, and a forward force of motion
Weight and the applied force only

diagnostic.prompt: In that situation, the normal force is:
options: Less than the weight - the rope's vertical component helps lift the box

physical_sciences.force_and_free_body_di.recap:
A force is a push or pull - an interaction between two objects - so every force on a diagram must have another object responsible for it. If you cannot name the object doing the pushing, the force does not exist. There is no "force of motion": motion needs no force to continue, only to CHANGE (Newton's first law).

Hunt forces systematically. Gravity first, always present: the weight w = mg, straight down (a 5 kg box weighs 5 × 9,8 = 49 N; mass in kilograms is a scalar and never changes, weight in newtons is a force). Then every touching object: a surface gives a normal force N perpendicular to itself, and friction f if rough; a rope gives tension along the rope; a hand gives an applied force. For a box pulled at constant velocity across a rough floor by a rope at 30° above the horizontal, the cast is exactly four: weight down, normal force up, applied force along the rope at the marked 30°, friction backward - because friction always opposes the sliding (or attempted sliding), not automatically the applied force.

A FREE-body diagram strips the scenery: the object becomes a dot, and only labelled force arrows remain, each starting on the dot, each with an arrowhead, angles marked. No floor, no rope, no velocity arrows - a velocity arrow drawn as a force costs marks.

The phrase "constant velocity" is physics in disguise: zero net force, everything balances, and the diagram becomes equations. A slanted force does two jobs at once, split into components: the rope pulls forward with F cos 30° and lifts with F sin 30°. Horizontal balance: F cos 30° = f. Vertical balance: N + F sin 30° = w - three players, not two. So the normal force is LESS than the weight here: the rope carries part of the load, and the floor pushes less. "N always equals w" is memorisation, not reading - N is whatever the vertical balance demands, case by case (push down on a box and N exceeds w). Since friction later scales with N, pulling at an upward angle genuinely makes dragging easier.

Method: isolate ONE object; hunt gravity then touches; draw the dot and labelled arrows; read the motion state (balanced, or net force with the acceleration); write the balances direction by direction.

exit_check.prompt: Why is there no forward 'force of motion' on the moving box?
options: Motion needs no force to continue - only changes of motion need force
It exists but is too small to draw

exit_check.prompt: 'Constant velocity' lets you write down that:
options: The forces balance in every direction - net force is zero

exit_check.prompt: Friction on an object always points:
options: Against the sliding (or attempted sliding) between the surfaces
Opposite to the applied force in all cases

exit_check.prompt: In a free-body diagram, the object is drawn as:
options: A dot with all labelled force arrows starting from it
A detailed sketch with the floor and rope

physical_sciences.formulae_and_balanced_.subject: Physical Sciences
physical_sciences.formulae_and_balanced_.subtopic: Balancing chemical equations; conservation of atoms and mass; law of constant composition
physical_sciences.formulae_and_balanced_.name: Writing formulae and balancing equations
physical_sciences.formulae_and_balanced_.example_problem: Write formulae for calcium chloride, ammonium sulphate and iron(III) oxide, then balance: C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O.
physical_sciences.formulae_and_balanced_.prior_knowledge: The periodic table; valency; cation and anion table

importance.summary: Underpins the entire Chemical Change section - 92/150 of the Gr 12 Paper 2, the single largest block in Physical Sciences - and every chemistry topic from Gr 11 term 3 onward.

required_by.topic: CHEMICAL CHANGE: Quantitative aspects of chemical change
CHEMICAL CHANGE: Rate and extent of reaction

covered_by.subtopic: Balancing chemical equations; conservation of atoms and mass; law of constant composition

diagnostic.prompt: The formula for iron(III) oxide is:
Balanced, the combustion of propane is:

physical_sciences.formulae_and_balanced_.recap:
Formula writing is charge arithmetic: an ionic compound must be electrically neutral, so the formula states the ratio of ions whose charges cancel to zero. Harvest charges from the periodic table and ion table: group 1 metals 1+, group 2 metals 2+, halogens 1−, group 16 nonmetals 2−. Calcium chloride: Ca²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ - CaCl₂. The crossover shortcut swaps each charge's size onto the other ion as a subscript, but always simplify afterwards (Mg²⁺ with O²⁻ crosses to Mg₂O₂, which reduces to MgO) and never write a subscript of 1.

Polyatomic ions are charged teams from the data sheet: ammonium NH₄⁺ (the rare positive one), sulphate SO₄²⁻ - the "-ate" ending signals oxygen aboard, unlike sulphide S²⁻. When a team takes a subscript, brackets are compulsory: ammonium sulphate is (NH₄)₂SO₄ - two nitrogens and eight hydrogens; without brackets the count collapses. Transition metals carry their charge in the name's Roman numeral: iron(III) means Fe³⁺, so iron(III) oxide balances 3+ against 2− at the lowest common multiple of six - Fe₂O₃ - while iron(II) oxide is the different compound FeO. Audit every formula: total plus must equal total minus.

Balancing enforces the law of conservation of mass: atoms are rearranged in reactions, never created or destroyed, so every element's count must match across the arrow. The one commandment: change only COEFFICIENTS, the multipliers in front of whole formulas - never subscripts, which define identity (edit H₂O to H₂O₂ and water has become peroxide; the equation now lies about the reaction).

For combustion, balance in the order carbon, hydrogen, oxygen - oxygen last because it appears in both products and stands alone as O₂, so one final coefficient settles it. Propane: C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Carbon: 3CO₂. Hydrogen: 4H₂O. Oxygen demanded on the right: 6 + 4 = 10 atoms, supplied in pairs: 5O₂. Balanced: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. If a half-coefficient appears (ethane needs 7/2 O₂), double every coefficient; final answers use the smallest whole-number set.

Never skip the closing audit - count each element aloud on both sides: C 3=3, H 8=8, O 10=10. Next step in the syllabus, those coefficients become mole ratios, so an unbalanced equation poisons every calculation built on it.

exit_check.prompt: Why must (NH₄)₂SO₄ keep its brackets?
options: The subscript 2 must multiply the whole ammonium team - 2 N and 8 H

exit_check.prompt: Why is 'balancing' an equation by changing H₂O to H₂O₂ illegal?
options: Subscripts define identity - that edit turns water into hydrogen peroxide
It is legal for oxygen only

exit_check.prompt: In combustion equations, oxygen is balanced last because:
options: It appears in both products and stands alone as O₂, so its count depends on the other coefficients

exit_check.prompt: The audit of C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O checks oxygen as:

physical_sciences.mole_concept.subject: Physical Sciences
physical_sciences.mole_concept.subtopic: The mole, Avogadro's number, molar mass
physical_sciences.mole_concept.name: The mole concept
physical_sciences.mole_concept.example_problem: Calculate the number of moles in 8,8 g of CO2, the number of molecules that represents, and the volume it occupies at STP.
physical_sciences.mole_concept.prior_knowledge: Relative atomic and molecular mass; formulae writing

importance.summary: Stoichiometry runs through the Chemical Change section (92/150 of the Gr 12 Paper 2) and is explicitly carried into the Gr 12 exam as 'stoichiometry, application only (Gr 11)'.

required_by.topic: CHEMICAL CHANGE: Quantitative aspects of chemical change

covered_by.topic: CHEMICAL CHANGE: Quantitative aspects of chemical change
covered_by.subtopic: The mole, Avogadro's number, molar mass

diagnostic.prompt: The number of moles in 8,8 g of CO₂ (M = 44 g/mol) is:
The volume that 0,2 mol of a gas occupies at STP is:

physical_sciences.mole_concept.recap:
Atoms are too small to count or weigh individually, yet reactions happen particle by particle - so chemistry counts in bulk, like eggs in dozens. One mole is 6,02 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number), sized so that one mole of a substance has a mass in grams equal to its relative molecular mass. That gram-mass of one mole is the molar mass M, in g/mol. Compute M from the formula, respecting subscripts: CO₂ is 12 + 2(16) = 44 g/mol - counting the doubled oxygen once (getting 28) is the classic wreck.

The central formula: n = m/M - moles equal the mass you have divided by the mass of one mole's worth. For 8,8 g of CO₂: n = 8,8/44 = 0,2 mol. Sense-check every division: 8,8 g is exactly one-fifth of 44 g, so one-fifth of a mole is right; 5 mol would imply 220 g.

From moles, two more roads open. Particles: N = n × Avogadro's number - 0,2 × 6,02 × 10²³ = 1,204 × 10²³ molecules; particle counts should be enormous, so a tiny answer means you divided when you should have multiplied. Gas volume: Avogadro's law says equal volumes of ANY gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules, so at STP (273 K, 101,3 kPa) one mole of any gas fills 22,4 dm³. V = n × 22,4 gives 0,2 × 22,4 = 4,48 dm³. The 22,4 shortcut is licensed ONLY for gases at STP - never liquids, solids, or other conditions.

Organise everything as the mole map: moles n at the centre, three roads out - to mass (× M), to particles (× 6,02 × 10²³), to gas volume at STP (× 22,4) - and the same roads inward by dividing. Every problem is a journey: travel IN from whatever the question gives (divide), then OUT along whichever road it wants (multiply). The 8,8 g problem entered from mass (÷44), and exited along both the particle road and the volume road.

Units discipline: mass in grams before n = m/M (convert kilograms first), volumes in dm³ (1 dm³ = 1 litre = 1 000 cm³ - convert once, at the end). Next term the balanced equation's coefficients become mole ratios, and this map powers all of stoichiometry.

exit_check.prompt: The molar mass of CO₂ is 44 g/mol because:
On the mole map, travelling INWARD to moles always means:
options: Dividing - by M, by Avogadro's number, or by 22,4

exit_check.prompt: The 22,4 dm³ molar volume may be used:
options: For any substance at any temperature

physical_sciences.vectors_and_scalars.subject: Physical Sciences
physical_sciences.vectors_and_scalars.name: Vectors and scalars
physical_sciences.vectors_and_scalars.example_problem: Classify displacement, speed, force, energy and velocity as vectors or scalars; then find the resultant of forces of 30 N east and 50 N west acting on the same object.

importance.summary: Foundation of Mechanics (65/150, Gr 12 Paper 1) and Electricity & Magnetism (55/150) - resultants and field/force directions are vector work throughout.

covered_by.subtopic: Physical quantities; vector vs scalar

diagnostic.prompt: Which classification is correct?
options: Vectors: displacement, force, velocity; scalars: speed, energy
Vectors: speed, energy; scalars: displacement, force, velocity

diagnostic.prompt: Forces of 30 N east and 50 N west act on the same object. The resultant is:

physical_sciences.vectors_and_scalars.recap:
Physics measures with two kinds of quantities. A scalar is complete with a magnitude and unit alone: mass, time, temperature, distance, speed, energy. A vector needs a magnitude AND a direction to mean anything: force, displacement, velocity, acceleration - a 30 N push east is an entirely different event from 30 N west. The test that never fails: does a direction make sense and is it NEEDED to complete the meaning? Never classify by how "powerful" a quantity sounds - energy has no direction, and 500 J northward is nonsense.

The famous pairs. Distance (scalar) counts every metre of the path; displacement (vector) compares only finish to start. One full 400 m track lap: distance 400 m, displacement zero. Speed (scalar) is how fast; velocity (vector) is speed with its direction - so that lap's average speed is 5 m/s while its average velocity is zero, because displacement was zero. The scalar tells how much moving happened; the vector tells the net effect.

Vectors demand their own arithmetic because directions can cancel. Adding along a line uses a sign convention: choose a positive direction, declare it, and stick to it. With east positive, 30 N east is +30 and 50 N west is −50. Add: +30 + (−50) = −20 - and translate the sign back: 20 N WEST. The resultant is the single vector with the same effect as all the originals together. The scalar reflex answer, 80 N, ignores that the forces fought: 30 N of the westward force was cancelled, and only 20 N survives. State every vector answer with magnitude AND direction - a bare number is half an answer.

Sanity checks: the resultant points with the larger force, and opposing magnitudes subtract. Special cases as landmarks: same direction - magnitudes add (the only case where the scalar reflex is right); equal and opposite - resultant zero, the equilibrium behind Newton's first law. The method scales to any number of forces on a line: declare positive, convert each to a signed number, add, translate back. Grade 11 extends this to two dimensions and components; the direction test and the sign convention travel with you all the way to matric.

exit_check.prompt: An athlete completes one full 400 m lap in 80 s. Average speed and average velocity are:
options: 5 m/s and zero - displacement is zero

exit_check.prompt: With east chosen positive, 30 N east and 50 N west become:
In which single case does adding magnitudes directly give the correct resultant?
options: When all vectors point in the same direction
